title: Nautical Travel Time Calculator: Knots to Hours
description: Work out sailing and boating time from nautical miles and knots with the Nautical Travel Time Calculator — passage hours for any steady speed. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 60-nautical-mile crossing at a steady 6 knots takes 10 hours on the calculator — the arithmetic every passage plan starts from, before weather gets its vote.
quick_answer: The Nautical Travel Time Calculator divides a distance in nautical miles by a speed in knots to give the passage time in hours. Enter the nautical miles and a realistic average speed and read the time — the starting estimate before currents and conditions adjust it.

faq: Should I enter speed through water or over ground?
Time comes from speed over ground. Currents and leeway make the two differ — a 2-knot adverse current turns a 6-knot boat into a 4-knot traveller, and the honest input is the 4.
Why does my real passage never match?
Averages hide slowdowns: harbour manoeuvres, traffic schemes, weather and tides. Experienced planners add a margin — 10–20% is the common habit — rather than trusting the bare division.
Divide the hours by 24: a 2,997-nautical-mile Atlantic crossing at 22 knots is 136 hours, about 5.7 days of steaming — port time excluded.
What speed do cargo ships actually make?
Typically 16–22 knots in service, slower when slow-steaming for fuel and emissions. The calculator takes whatever service speed your source quotes.
Can I work in kilometres instead?
Convert first — one nautical mile is exactly 1.852 km — or keep the whole problem nautical: miles, knots and hours are one consistent system, which is its charm.
The same division applies with ground speed; airliners plan on forecast winds exactly as sailors plan on currents. This page's marine framing is the arithmetic's home, not its limit.
Price each leg separately and add the hours — the total is the sum of leg times, never total distance ÷ average of speeds.
